Three doors down on Day 128 set the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light, opened no slate, turned no errand into a walk to Slate Row and stood a half-pace off while Alda laid her birth-slates before the fold, asked nothing about the sign, the date, the tin or the six pages. At the fire on all three days told it the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it} where another woman would say \emph{I}, stood counting under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale in the dying light, set the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand and did not look toward the bed; the payer went unnamed for a hundred and twenty-eight days (T088). Within hearing of Tarn’s second stopping she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing; she did not ask Jorra about the men, his dust or his finger in the damper, and neither man named the other’s silence. Widow’s mark untouched at a rack, a strip, a well, a yard, a market, a road, a basket, a bed and a dusk, because none was an opening. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands and nothing was explained.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 30: Days 129–131, Reed 10–12. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Cross, the kiln-house, House Silt three doors down and back under the roof, set him on his bed under the roof and not in the Debt Loft each dusk, put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without a look at his face, left the thread frozen and unwiped, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting before it went away. Gave the instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket; said \emph{the house}; went wide around the rack space where the broken birth-slates lie and around the place where a hand went in on Seed 15 and did not come back. At the Cross on Day 129 set the basket in the moot-post’s shade where no slate lay and stood a half-pace off while Berr read his figure over the crowd. In the kiln-house she set the basket low near the bench leg at the angle where a child sees the underside of the shelf, told the fire it was the thaw, and sent a neighbour with a wet pot to the pot with \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}, her hand going once to the clay jar and coming away (T058/T079, T077). \textbf{On Day 131 she stood at the shelf with her back to the basket, moved her lips along the row with two gaps, and reached a finger beneath the board where the charcoal tally lies, without looking at it and without a word, then brought it away; she did not go back to the shelf that night (T100 carried, unexplained).} At the fire on all three days told it it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale, set the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand and did not look toward the bed; the payer went unnamed for one hundred and twenty-nine, one hundred and thirty and one hundred and thirty-one days (T088). Within hearing of Tarn’s third stopping on Day 130 she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing; she did not ask Jorra about the men or his dust, and neither man named the other’s silence. Widow’s mark untouched at a shelf, an afternoon and a dusk, because none was an opening. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands and nothing was explained.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 31: Days 132–134, Reed 13–15, on stage all three days. Carried him at the half-pace from every open slate to the Clay Yard, the reed beds’ edge, the loaf shelf and the hearth, the road downriver and back, the Cross and the market stalls, the fish-trade shade below the sill, and up the clay road to his bed under the roof each dusk, never into the Debt Loft; put the fold right at his ear and under his chin without looking at his face, left the thread frozen, her hand resting a half-beat longer than the setting before it went away. Instruction to the wool, the river wind, the pot, the broom and the fire and never to the basket; \emph{the house} where another woman says \emph{I}. Went around the clean dark line, the new finer grey called the thaw, the rack space with its broken birth-slates and the empty place in the returning line with a look and a wide step and no number (T009/T013/T092, T098 carried). \textbf{On Day 132 set the basket low at the angle where the underside of the shelf becomes a roof and, with her back to it and her lips moving along the row with its two gaps, reached a finger beneath the board where the charcoal tally lies, without looking and without a word, and brought it away; on Day 134, glancing once at the clay jar cold under its glaze, she did it again and again did not go back to the shelf (T100 carried, unexplained).} To the neighbour with dry mud in her wrists who asked what the row would want before the tend was out, \emph{Ask the pot what a wet thing costs set down there. The house has said it}; to the man who asked what the reeds would want, the weather and the river, never a figure (T058/T079, T077). Before first grey on Day 133 three or four men with their collars high went low into the finger’s-width-open room off the shed; she carried past, turned no head, gave them no name and did not say the room was cold (T035/T031). Within hearing of Tarn’s \textbf{fourth} stopping that night she gave the end of her instruction to the pot and asked nothing; she did not ask Jorra about the men or the dust and he did not ask about the ear, and the two silences stayed unjoined (T036/T076). At the fire on all three days told it it was the thaw, turned the coals with the back of a broken pot, said \emph{The house will keep it}, counted under her breath toward no opening, pushed coal-black hair back with the burn-wrist, the grey streak pale, set the pot rim out and handle toward the reaching hand two inches beyond it and did not look toward the bed; the payer went unnamed for one hundred and thirty-two, one hundred and thirty-three and one hundred and thirty-four days (T088). Widow’s mark untouched at a shelf, an afternoon, a strip, a rack, a basket, a bed and a dusk, because none was an opening. No new scar or possession, no bond changed hands and nothing was explained.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 32: Days 135–137, Reed 16–18, on stage all three days. \CRcharacter*{Alda Reed}{the hearth-maid who crossed herself and told nobody}{build/art/characters/alda-reed.png}{\CRfield{Also called}{Alda, Alda the hearth-maid, the keeper of the second notes}\CRfield{Role}{ally}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 770, Low Kiln, Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic)}\CRfield{Origin}{Low Kiln, Sill, Grath; House Reed}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the Hearth-Maids; birth-slates of Low Kiln; collector’s assistant at Sill}\CRfield{Status}{alive — six pages unread, the sixth written on Day 64, at the close of Day 146 (on stage briefly on Day 146, three doors down in House Silt)}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 1}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Forty-two and built like a woman who has spent her life lifting other people’s children: broad shoulders, a permanent stoop from leaning over births, and hands so steady that a mother will grab her wrist rather than her arm when the pain comes. Her nails are scrubbed to the quick and still have clay under them. She wears a grey wool shawl in every season and a little tin box on a cord inside her bodice, which she touches when a question is asked and never opens in company. She smells of soap, warm milk, tallow and the faint mineral tang of the Ash she has promised herself she will sweep tomorrow. The thing people notice first is her calm; the thing they notice last is the crossed sign she makes with two fingers at the corner of a birth-flower, which she does not know she does in front of strangers.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Practical instruction in proverbs and half-sentences. She addresses the newborn, the stone, the slip, the mother, and only then the father, in that order. She does not say \emph{please} and she does not say \emph{sorry}, and she does not consider this coldness; she considers it the correct amount of words for a room where somebody is in pain. She has a habit of answering a question with the date. When she is lying she becomes unusually exact.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “Warm the stone first. A cold stone is a stone, not a kindness.”

\item “Don’t set that near the fire. You’ll pay for it in the thaw.”

\item “He grew worse on the third day. So did the one before him. That’s all I’ve written.”

\item “The Court struck the name out. They didn’t strike the child out.”

\item “I crossed myself. It’s what my mother did. Don’t make it more than that.”

\item “In the levy. Among the children taken for the account this month.” --- the lie, delivered as an entry and never as a story.

\item “A woman with a thin return goes asking after the levy and a hand comes down on a slate that was better left where it lay.” --- mercy spoken in the grammar of a warning.

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born in Low Kiln to a family of reed-cutters and became a hearth-maid at nineteen, which in Grath means midwife, keeper of the birth-slate, and the person a household calls before it calls a collector. She has attended something over four hundred births. The first of the second notes was not hers. In Y.H. 651, long before she was born, a hearth-maid in Low Kiln attended an infant who grew worse on the third day and spoke words in a language no one in the district knew. The Court’s physician at Greybank wrote it down as a settling of the graft, struck the phrase \emph{Second Want} from his own report, and paid the maid for her trouble. That note passed down the order, from hand to hand and tin to tin, until it came to Alda. She has added to it every year since she took it up: every infant who grew worse on the third day, every word that did not belong to Grathic, every birth-flower shaped like a branch instead of a rose. The notes live under a floorboard in her house, in a second hand that the Court has never seen. Alda Reed’s is the fullest set in the order.

She attended Enna Vail’s death in Y.H. 804 and sat with Sella through a night in which nothing she did mattered. She attended Corin’s birth on Stone 7, Y.H. 812, crossed herself at the branching red flower across his ribs, and told nobody what she had seen. Three days later she told Dessa Silt that her child had gone in the levy, which was a lie told to keep a whole-return infant off a slate that every officer in Slate Row would have wanted to read. She has not slept properly since.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
Four hundred births and one she cannot account for. On Day 1 the sign is made in front of witnesses and covered with a word and a date nobody asked for; from that hour she is a woman who has hidden a thing in a room where everybody is arranging silence. She fears collectors — not their tubes, which she has held, but their slates, which are always in a better hand than hers. She fears that the second notes are a treasonous thing and that keeping them has made her a person who waits for children to get worse. She fears Dessa’s face in the street. Her contradiction: the woman who insists that everything be written down within three days has spent thirty years keeping a second record that cannot be shown to anyone, and calls it \emph{not wanting trouble}.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants one of the Court’s physicians to read her notes and say the words she struck out herself. She thinks she wants the boy she delivered to grow up ordinary, so that she can stop looking at him. What she needs is to understand that she has been a keeper of the truth in the only way available to a hearth-maid: badly, in secret, and at a cost to the woman she lied to.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Corin} — the child she delivered and crossed herself over. She has watched him for three years without once saying what she saw, and has begun to suspect he knows that she knows. \emph{Ch 1:} she lifted him, cleaned him in a deliberate order (face, neck, groin, knees, cord), pressed the wool flat with the same two fingers that had made the sign, and would not say his name. \emph{Ch 2:} she washed him in the same order on the second morning, reached for the slate first and pushed the writing further under, touched the tin at her bodice, and made the crossed sign again at the corner of the flower without knowing she was doing it in front of him. She said warm and breathing was all she had set down, which was not true. \emph{Ch 3:} at the fringe of the market she kept the birth-slates in a row, turning the writing down when a mother came near. She stopped at the basket to straighten the bottom slate, touched the tin inside her bodice a third time, saw the red branching edge of the flower at his wrist where the wool had ridden back, and crossed two fingers at the corner of it before she knew she had done it in front of a market full of people. She covered the sign with a date nobody had asked for: \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out.}

\textbf{Sella Vail} — they have traded a silence since the boy was three days old. Sella has never asked what Alda wrote; Alda has never asked why Sella took the child. This is not friendship. It is an arrangement with a door in it that both women have agreed not to open. \emph{Ch 1:} the arrangement begins in the birth room, before a word is spoken between them: Alda lays the slate flat as the hand in the door goes back out. \emph{Ch 2:} when Sella came for the boy she put her hand near the slate on the bench and did not touch it, and neither woman looked at the other. The arrangement holds. \emph{Ch 3:} at the market’s edge the two women are a pace apart without a word passing: Sella’s little-door hand closes the wool over the red edge of the flower, and a few paces away the collector’s clerk’s hand closes on his slate. Both are careful hands entering the same child in two different accounts, and neither account has been shown to him.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — she lied to this woman about her own child and has taken her barley money from Sella’s house ever since. When Dessa speaks to her in the street, Alda answers with the weather and hates the sound of her own voice. \emph{Ch 1:} she delivered Dessa’s child and met the unasked question with dates and weather, her hand on the slate rather than on the mother. \emph{Ch 2:} she stood behind Dessa in the Clay Yard as the bundle went up the hill and told her the boy had gone in the levy among the children taken for the account; she became exact about dates nobody had asked for, and the figure was never spoken. The lie is told to keep a slate unread and has begun to curdle.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — they work the same room standing and trade small facts at the door. \emph{Ch 1:} neither sat where the slate lay open, and each kept her face arranged for the other. \emph{Ch 2:} Mira is not in the room; her crust of brown-edged barley is the last warmth that crossed it from her hands.

\textbf{Jorra Vail} — he knows she wrote something down the night Enna died and has never asked to see it. She has begun to be afraid of the day he does, because the boy in his house is the one thing Jorra could be persuaded to burn for.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — pays her to keep the birth-slates and has never asked about the second notes. She has decided this is because he knows and does not want a copy of anything, which may be true.

\textbf{Orra Weir} — was in the room on Stone 7 and tied a knot she cannot account for. They never discuss it. Orra is the only person Alda has ever let near the subject of the third day, and even she has not seen the tin.

\textbf{Ch 4.} The arrangement with Sella held in the death-house by a half-pace and a slate turned writing-down: she wrote what she did not leave lying about and Sella did not ask. With the neighbour mother she gave dates where comfort was asked for and a graft settling where an answer was wanted, and the woman wrapped the feet. With Dessa there was no meeting at all this chapter; the lie is three days old and already a fact in the woman’s face. She touched the tin twice and crossed the sign twice more without knowing she did it in front of a room and a basket.

\textbf{Ch 6.} She came under the Vail roof at mid-morning of Stone 16 to see the child she delivered, smelling of soap and warm milk, and reached for her slate before she reached for him. She laid the birth-slates writing-down on the bench, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder longer than a fold required, touched the tin once inside her bodice, crossed two fingers at the red edge of the flower at his wrist without knowing she did it, and covered the sign with \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out} and then with dates nobody had asked for. On her own narrow slate she wrote what she did not leave lying about and turned it writing-down into her shawl, toward a floorboard in her house he does not know, and went on giving exact dates after the question had stopped. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} she answered \emph{Warm and breathing --- that’s all I’ve set down}, which was exact and not true.

\textbf{Ch 7.} On Stone 24 she came under the Vail roof smelling of lye and milk warmed for somebody else’s child, laid the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, and pressed the fold flat too long at his shoulder. Her hand went once to the tin inside her bodice and came away without opening it. She made the two-finger sign at the red edge of the birth-flower at his wrist before she knew she had done it, and covered it with the same unasked-for date she had given Dessa --- Stone seven, the account up on the eighth --- and went on with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End and the potter’s third child in Stonemouth after there was no question left to answer. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} she said \emph{Warm and breathing, that’s all I’ve set down}, exact and untrue. On a narrow slate she wrote what she would not leave lying, in a second hand no Court physician had seen, and turned it writing-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in a house the boy could not name: a further note for the tin, still unread. Dessa’s cough three doors down went on being weather, and the lie went on standing.

\textbf{Ch 8.} On the Long Night she sat under the Vail roof with the fire out and told the story of the hearth-maid’s account in which dates stand where wonder should be, going on after the question had stopped, and did not know she had made the sign at the red edge of his wrist. On the Remembering she came with birth-slates and the smell of soap and warm milk, laid dates where a name should stand, touched the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, pressed the fold flat too long at his shoulder and crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knew she had done it, then covered the sign with the same unasked-for date she had given Dessa. No note was written this chapter and the tin stayed shut; she went home to a house the boy cannot name and was offstage on the Last Day and Ilmen 1.

\textbf{Ch 9.} On Ilmen 5 she came under the Vail roof smelling of soap and warm milk, laid the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder longer than a fold required, touched the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, and crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower at his wrist before she knew she had done it. She covered the sign with the same unasked-for date she had given Dessa --- Stone seven, the account up on the eighth --- and went on with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End and a potter’s third child in Stonemouth after there was no question left to answer. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} she said \emph{Warm and breathing --- that’s all I’ve set down}, which was exact and not true. On a narrow slate she wrote what she would not leave lying, in a second hand no Court physician had seen, and turned it writing-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in a house the boy could not name: a fourth note for the tin, still unread.

\textbf{Ch 10.} She comes after the vessel has given, not before: soap and warm milk gone cold under river silt, lye and wet wool and the mineral edge of the water on her. She goes to a narrow slate before she goes to the body, lays it writing-down on a flat stone at the edge of the bank, touches the little tin once inside her bodice without opening it, and only then turns to the woman and the basket. She does not say the woman’s name. She lays dates where a wonder should have stood --- Stone seven, the account up on the eighth, a cooper’s seventh, a potter’s third child --- going on after there was no question left to answer, because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. The lie told for mercy has now become a fact in a dead woman’s face that nobody can correct, and she has not slept well since the day she told it. On Ilmen 14 she stands beside Orra Weir in the lee of the Eel House with soap-and-milk still on her, gives the date of the last high water where the other woman says the river is up, touches the tin once and comes away empty, and lets a number for the traps change into weather rather than say the third day. She writes no new note this chapter; the tin stays shut.

\textbf{Ch 11.} She came short under the roof at mid-morning of Day 46 with soap-and-warm-milk gone cold under river silt and lye under the soap, the birth-slates under her arm. She laid the slates writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder a breath too long, touched the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knew she had done it, and covered the sign with the same unasked-for date she gave Dessa. She went on giving dates after there was no question left to stop her --- the cooper’s seventh in Mud End, a potter’s third child in Stonemouth, the last high water --- and said \emph{Warm and breathing --- that’s all I’ve set down}, which was exact and not true. She did not say the woman’s name, did not say the third day and wrote no new note. The lie told for mercy is six days old and has curdled all the way through to a death nobody entered, and no living person can correct it.

\textbf{Ch 12.} On Day 51 she laid the birth-slates writing-down before she turned to the fold, pressed the fold too long, touched the tin once unopened and crossed the sign at the flower’s red edge without knowing it, covering it with the date she gave Dessa; Sella stood a half-pace off and did not ask. Dessa is eleven days in the ground and the lie told for mercy has curdled all the way through to a death nobody entered; the name and the third day were not said. With Mira she trades small facts standing up; nothing was asked by Jorra or Berr about the fifth note turned toward the floorboard. Her hand is one of three the boy keeps on a tray and does not turn into a cause.

\textbf{Ch 13.} On Ilmen 27 she came short into House Silt with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye sour under the soap, the birth-slates under her arm. She laid the slates writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder a breath longer than a fold required, made the two-finger sign at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knew she had done it and covered it with the same unasked-for date she gave Dessa. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} she said \emph{warm and breathing}, exact and not true, and went on with dates after there was no question left to answer. She touched the tin inside her bodice without opening it and wrote no sixth note this chapter; the hidden record stays at five, turned face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, and the sixth page waits for Day 64. She did not say the woman’s name or the third day, and the lie told for mercy has curdled through to a death twenty-two mornings old that no living person can correct.

\textbf{Ch 14.} On Silt 5 she came short into House Silt with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye sour under the soap, the birth-slates under her arm, and laid the writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold. She pressed the fold flat at his shoulder a breath longer than a fold requires, touched the little tin inside her bodice once without opening it, crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knew she had done it, and covered the sign with the date she gave Dessa — Stone seven, the account up on the eighth. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} she said \emph{warm and breathing}, exact and not true, and went on with a cooper’s seventh in Mud End and a potter’s third child in Stonemouth after there was no question left to answer. Then she wrote the withheld sixth note in the second hand on a narrow slate and turned it face-down into her grey shawl toward a floorboard in a house the boy could not name. The hidden record grew from five pages to six, unread, and bought no recognition. Two private records in two materials stood in one room on separate trays and were read by nobody, and the mercy-lie curdled through to a woman twenty-six mornings dead that no living person could correct.

\textbf{Ch 15.} She is offstage through the flood, and the record she keeps goes on without her. On Silt 13 the sixth narrow page still lies turned face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, written in the second hand on Day 64 and read by nobody, and the little tin stays shut inside her bodice; three doors down the pewter tin above the empty bed keeps its pale fold and thumb-bright rub, unopened. Two private records in two materials stand unread while the water goes down, and neither carries either to a door. The narrow page is not written again, the tin is not opened, and no living person can correct the mercy-lie against a woman thirty-six mornings dead and uncollected; the number stays in Dessa’s thumb and the name under the sieve-wire scar and the third day is still unsaid. Her hand is one of three the boy keeps on a tray and does not turn into a cause.

\textbf{Ch 16.} On Day 76, Silt 17, she comes short three doors down in House Silt with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye sour under the soap, the birth-slates under her arm. She lays the writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, presses the fold flat at his shoulder a breath longer than a fold requires, crosses two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knows she has done it, and covers the sign with the date she gave Dessa --- the seventh of Stone, the account up on the eighth. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} she says \emph{Warm and breathing, that’s all I’ve set down}, exact and not true for three years, and goes on with dates after the question has stopped. Her hand goes once to the little tin inside her bodice and comes away without opening it. Her sixth narrow slate stays turned face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, written in the second hand on Day 64 and read by nobody; the hidden record stands at six pages and no seventh is written. Two private records in two materials --- the pewter tin above the empty bed with its pale fold and thumb-bright rub, and the turned slate toward the floorboard --- stand apart in one room over a woman thirty-nine mornings dead and uncollected, and neither is carried to a door or read by anybody. The mercy-lie has curdled past correction and no living person can take the date off the sign.

\textbf{Ch 17.} On Silt 21, three doors down in House Silt, she lays her birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, presses the fold too long at his shoulder, crosses two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower without knowing it and covers the sign with the date she gave Dessa — the seventh of Stone, the account up on the eighth — a date that now stands over a woman forty mornings dead and uncollected, which no living person can take off. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} she says \emph{Warm and breathing, that’s all I’ve set down}, exact and not true, and goes on with dates after the question has stopped, because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. Her hand goes once to the little tin in her bodice and comes away without opening it. Her sixth narrow slate stays turned face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, written on Day 64 and read by nobody: six pages, all unread, no seventh written and T023 not paid again. She does not say the woman’s name or the third day, and does not open either tin.

\textbf{Ch 20 (bonds).} With Corin the order of reaching is unchanged: the birth-slates go down on the bench before the fold is pressed, and the sign at the flower’s red edge is made before she knows it and covered with the date she gave Dessa. With Sella a half-pace and a turned slate stand in for the arrangement again; neither asked about the sign, the date, the tin or the sixth page. Dessa is more mornings dead than any living person keeps count of, lies uncollected, and the lie told for mercy is a fact no living person can take off the sign; her number, name and third day were not said. Mira and Orra remain offstage, their boards and cords unread, and Jorra and Berr asked nothing of her writing. No tin was opened, no seventh note written and no bond paid this chapter.

The round pewter tin above the abandoned board-bed kept its pale fold at the seam and its thumb-bright rub, unopened, and the grey wool below held only the hollow where the small pale river stone had lain; nobody said either was gone. Sella stood a half-pace off with the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light and asked nothing about the writing, the tin, the sign or the date. No tin was opened, no seventh note written and no bond paid.

\CRsheetheading{Arc So Far}
The two gestures that will define her are on the page in Chapter 1: the crossed sign she does not know she makes in front of strangers, and the exact, unasked-for dates with which she covers it. In Chapter 2 both gestures repeat and a third is added. She reaches for the slate before the child again, touches the little tin on its cord twice more, crosses the sign over the flower in front of the boy without knowing it, and answers every unasked question with an exact history --- a cooper’s seventh in Mud End, the account going up on the eighth before the paper went out --- until the dates arrive faster than dates have any business arriving. Then she tells Dessa the boy went in the levy. The lie is told as mercy and cannot be undone. In Chapter 3 she keeps the birth-slates at the edge of the market, touches the tin a third time and makes the sign a third time in front of witnesses, and the date she uses to cover it is the same one she gave Dessa: the account up on the eighth, before the paper went out. The market goes on around the sign and the date and the red edge at a wrist, arranging itself around the things it does not read. The tin under the floorboard is years away from being read.

On Days 5 and 6 the tin is touched twice more and the second notes acquire a second hiding place. She comes under the Vail roof to look at the child she delivered, reaches for the slate before him, presses the fold at his shoulder too long, crosses the sign at the red edge of his wrist without knowing she does it in front of him, and answers a mother’s three questions with exact dates and a graft settling. In the death-house she sets her own slate writing-down on the bench and then writes a second note that she turns down and slides under a milk cup, where no mother and no officer will think to pick it up. She crosses her fingers again at a red mark at a rekindled child’s hairline without knowing it. The Court’s struck word is still not spoken in the room; the kindest voice in it is closing a question nobody opened, and the boy knows the shape of the gesture and has no sentence for it.

On Days 10 through 14 the lie and the writing go on together. She comes under the Vail roof on Stone 16 and reaches for the slate before the child, presses the fold flat too long, touches the tin once, crosses the sign at the red edge of his wrist without knowing it and covers it with the same unasked-for date she gave Dessa, then with more dates after the question has stopped. On a narrow slate she writes a second note of what she will not leave lying about and turns it face-down into her shawl, toward a floorboard in her house the boy cannot name; the note and the warmth of the fold are one gesture. The tin stays inside her bodice, unopened; neither this note nor the one under the milk cup in the death-house has been read. \emph{Warm and breathing} is said exactly and is a lie, and the sign is made a further time in front of a child who cannot hand it back.

On Days 15 through 24 the lie and the writing go on together and the hidden record grows another page. On Stone 24 she reaches for the slate before the child, touches the unopened tin, presses the fold too long, crosses the sign at the red edge of the flower without knowing it and covers it with the date she gave Dessa, then pours out dates after the question has stopped. She writes a further note that she does not leave lying and turns it face-down toward the floorboard, so that a third hidden record goes where no officer’s thumb will look. The boy cannot read Grathic, cannot ask which house holds the floorboard, cannot hand the gesture back; he keeps the sign and the turned slate beside the dust from the back room as two truths arranged in one morning by women who are kind. Dessa coughs from the pits three doors down and calls it weather, and the lie told for mercy is still a fact in her face. The tin stays shut and none of the notes has been read.

On Days 25 through 30 the lie and the gestures go on without the writing. On the Long Night she gives dates where wonder should stand in a story told in the dark, and the boy files the gap after the question with the intervals; on the Remembering she comes under the Vail roof with the birth-slates, lays a date where a name should stand, touches the tin once unopened and crosses two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower without knowing it, covering the sign with the same date she gave Dessa. She is offstage on the Last Day and Ilmen 1. The boy cannot read Grathic, cannot ask which house holds the floorboard and cannot hand the gesture back; he keeps the sign and the date beside the unspoken name as truths arranged by a woman who is kind. The tin stays shut, no further note is written, and the lie told to Dessa for mercy is still a fact in her face.

On Days 31 through 37 the lie and the writing go on together and the hidden record grows a fourth page. On Ilmen 5 she reaches for the slate before the child, touches the unopened tin, presses the fold too long, crosses the sign at the red edge of the flower without knowing it and covers it with the date she gave Dessa, then pours out dates after the question has stopped. She writes a fourth note that she does not leave lying and turns it face-down toward the floorboard, so that another page goes where no officer’s thumb will look. Three doors down Dessa’s cough is worse and is called weather, and the note under the milk cup, the notes under the floorboard and the tin inside the bodice stay shut. The boy cannot read Grathic, cannot ask which house holds the floorboard and cannot hand the gesture back; he keeps the sign and the turned slate as two truths arranged in one morning by a woman who is kind.

On Days 38 through 44 the lie curdles against the death it was told to hide, and the writing goes on without the writing-down. On Ilmen 9 she came down from the road after the vessel had given, with lye and wet wool and the mineral edge of river water instead of soap and warm milk, and went to a narrow slate before she went to the body, laying it writing-down on a flat stone at the bank; her hand went once inside her bodice and touched the tin without opening it, and she did not say the woman’s name. She laid dates where a wonder should have stood and went on after there was no question left to answer; the boy lay in the basket on the bank and watched the order of reaching. On Ilmen 14 she came up the river road with soap-and-milk still on her and stood with Orra Weir in the lee of the Eel House, saying the date of the last high water where Orra said the river was up. Her hand went into her bodice once and came out empty; when a figure came near, she said the weather had turned and Orra said the river would do what the river did, and the subject changed so neatly nobody could have said it had been there. Nothing was said of the third day, no note was written, and the tin stayed shut while the lie she told for mercy became a fact nobody could correct.

On Days 45 through 47 the lie curdles and the gestures go on without the writing-down. On Day 46 she comes under the Vail roof with the birth-slates and reaches for them before she reaches for the child, presses the fold too long, touches the tin once and does not open it, makes the two-finger sign at the red edge of the flower without knowing it and covers it with the date she gave Dessa. The dates go on arriving after the question has stopped because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry; \emph{warm and breathing} is exact and not true, and the death it can no longer be corrected against is six days old. She writes no new note and the tin stays shut. Three doors down the woman who believed the lie has been in the ground nine mornings, and the boy lies in a fold from which the smoky crust has quietly gone; she is one of the three hands he sets on a tray and refuses to turn into a cause.

On Days 48 through 54 the lie curdles and the gestures go on without the writing-down until a fifth page is added. On Day 51 she comes short under the Vail roof with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye under the soap, lays the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, presses the fold flat at his shoulder a breath too long, touches the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, and makes the two-finger sign at the flower’s red edge before she knows she has done it, covering it with the date she gave Dessa. The dates go on arriving after the question has stopped --- a cooper’s seventh in Mud End, a potter’s third child in Stonemouth, the last high water --- because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. She says \emph{Warm and breathing}, exact and not true, does not say the woman’s name or the third day, and writes a fifth note in the second hand which she turns face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name. The lie told for mercy is eleven days old and has curdled all the way through to a death nobody entered that no living person can correct.

On Days 55 through 60 the lie curdles and the gestures go on without the writing-down. On Ilmen 27 she comes short under the roof three doors down with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye under the soap, lays the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, presses the fold flat at his shoulder a breath too long, crosses two fingers at the red edge of the flower before she knows she has done it and covers the sign with the date she gave Dessa, then goes on with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End and a potter’s third child in Stonemouth after there is no question left to answer. \emph{Warm and breathing} is said exactly and is not true; she touches the little tin inside her bodice without opening it, does not say the woman’s name or the third day, and writes no sixth note, so the hidden record stays at five and the sixth page waits for another week. Above the empty bed the pewter tin with its pale fold and thumb-bright lid keeps its place and neither tin is opened; two private records in two materials stand in one room on separate trays and are read by nobody. The lie told for mercy is now curdled all the way through to a death twenty-two mornings old that nobody entered and no living person can correct. Her hand is one of the three the boy keeps on a tray and does not turn into a cause.

On Days 61 through 67 the lie curdles and the hidden record gains its sixth page. On Silt 5 she comes short into the death-house room three doors down with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye sour under the soap, lays the birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, presses the fold too long, touches the tin inside her bodice without opening it, crosses two fingers at the flower’s red edge without knowing it and covers the sign with the date she gave Dessa. \emph{Warm and breathing} is said exactly and is not true, and no living person can correct it against a woman twenty-six mornings dead. She goes on with her exact dates after the question has stopped, because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. Then, on the narrow slate, she writes in the second hand what she will not leave lying and turns it face-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name: the sixth page, paid on Day 64 and read by nobody. Above the board-bed the pewter tin keeps its pale fold and thumb-bright lid, and in the fold of grey wool where the small pale river stone once lay there is only the hollow, which neither the house nor the boy mentions. Two private records in two materials stand in one room on separate trays, and she goes home to a house he cannot enter, with the date still laid over the sign and the number and the third day still unsaid.

On Days 68 through 74 the lie curdles against a death thirty-six mornings old and the writing stays where it is. She is offstage through the flood, and the sixth page written on Silt 5 lies turned face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, unread, while the little tin stays shut inside her bodice; three doors down the pewter tin above the empty bed keeps its pale fold and thumb-bright lid and nobody opens it. Two private records in two materials stand unread while the water rises and falls, and neither is carried to a door. The narrow page is not written again, the tin is not opened, and no living person can correct the mercy-lie told for a child who was never among the Forty. The number stays in Dessa’s thumb and the name under the sieve-wire scar and the third day is still unsaid, and her hand is one of three on the tray the boy refuses to turn into a cause.

On Days 75 through 77 the lie curdles against a death thirty-nine mornings old and the writing stays where it is. She comes short on Silt 17, lays the slates down before the fold, presses the fold too long, crosses the sign unknowing and covers it with the date given to Dessa; \emph{warm and breathing} is exact and not true, and she goes on with dates after the question stops because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. The sixth page written on Day 64 is not written again and is not paid again; the little tin and the pewter tin above the empty bed stay shut. Two private records in two materials stand unread in one room and are carried to no door, and the boy cannot enter either. Her hand stays on the tray with Sella’s and Mira’s and does not become a cause.

The date she laid over the sign now stands over a woman forty mornings dead and uncollected and cannot be taken off by any living person; the number stays in Dessa’s thumb, the name under the sieve-wire scar, the third day unsaid. On Days 85 through 90 the lie curdles against a death more mornings gone than any living person keeps count of, and the writing stays where it is. To the question she says \emph{Warm and breathing, that’s all I’ve set down}, exact and not true, and goes on with dates after the question has stopped, because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. Her hand goes once to the little tin in her bodice and comes away without opening it; her sixth narrow slate stays face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, six pages in the second hand all unread, no seventh written and T023 not paid again. Above the abandoned bed the round pewter tin keeps its pale fold at the seam and its thumb-bright rub, unopened, and the grey wool below holds only the hollow where the small pale river stone lay; nobody says either is gone. Two private records in two materials stand apart in one room, read by nobody and carried to no door. Sella stands a half-pace off with the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door and turns no errand into a walk to Slate Row; the number, the name and the third day remain unsaid and no living person can take the date off the sign.

The mercy-lie curdles one day further against a death nobody can correct, and the two-finger sign and the exact date go on together without her knowing either. Six pages in a second hand and the pewter tin above the empty bed stand apart in one room, read by nobody, carried to no door; no seventh page has been written. The cooper’s seventh in Mud End and the potter’s third child in Stonemouth are dates given after the question stopped, a handle on a thing too large to carry.

On Day 146 the lie curdles further against a death no living person can correct and the writing stays where it is. She appears once, at midday three doors down in House Silt, and is offstage by evening. She comes short with soap-and-milk gone cold under river silt and lye sour under the soap, nails scrubbed to the quick with clay still under them, and lays her birth-slates writing-down on the bench before she turns to the fold, the order of a hand that reaches for the record before a person. She presses the wool flat at his shoulder a breath longer than a fold requires, crosses two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knows she has done it and covers the sign with the date she gave Dessa — \emph{Stone seven. The account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out} — now standing over a woman more mornings dead than any living person keeps count of and uncollected, which no living person can take off. To Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet} she says \emph{Warm and breathing, that’s all I’ve set down}, exact and not true, and goes on with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End, a potter’s third child in Stonemouth and the last high water after the question has stopped, because dates are a handle on a thing too large to carry. Her hand goes once into her bodice to the little tin and comes away without opening it; her sixth narrow slate stays face-down toward a floorboard in a house the boy cannot name, six pages in a second hand all unread, no seventh written and T023 not paid again. The round pewter tin above the abandoned board-bed keeps its pale fold at the seam and its thumb-bright rub, unopened, and the grey wool below holds only the hollow where the small pale river stone had lain; nobody says either is gone. Two private records in two materials stand apart in one room, read by nobody and carried to no door; the number, the name and the third day stay unsaid and no living person can take the date off the sign. Sella stands a half-pace off with the basket just inside the finger’s-width-open door at the edge of the light and asks nothing. No tin opened, no new note written, no new scar or possession.

\CRsheetheading{Chapter Log}
\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 1: Delivered Corin in the front room of House Silt and worked with steady hands, clay under her nails. Reached for the slate before the child. Put her two fingers to the branching flower, noticed she had done it before witnesses, and covered the act with \emph{birth-flower} plus an unasked-for history from Nine Pots: Y.H. 806, fourth day of Stone, a potter’s third child, now a carter in Stonemouth. Touched the tin at her bodice twice. Gave a date and a weather report for the unasked question and said warm and breathing was all she had set down. Closed the slate flat on the bench while Sella Vail’s hand hovered in the door.

\item Ch 2: On Day 2 washed the child in her order, reached for the slate first, touched the tin a further time, made the crossed sign over the flower before witnesses without knowing it, and gave a date and weather where comfort was expected. On Day 3 stood behind Dessa at the end of the Clay Yard and told her the boy was entered in the levy among the children taken for the account that month, that the account went up on the eighth before the paper went out, and that a woman with a thin return who goes asking draws a hand down on a slate better left where it lay. Said warm and breathing was all she had set down. The number was never spoken; she went on giving dates after the question had stopped.

\item Ch 3: Day 4, Account-day. Kept the birth-slates under her arm and in a row on a bench at the fringe of the market, turning the writing down when a mother came near. Touched the tin inside her bodice once, the third sighting of it, when there was no question in the air to answer. Saw the edge of the birth-flower at the boy’s wrist, crossed two fingers at the corner of it without knowing she had done it in front of a market full of people, and covered the sign with an exact, unasked-for date: \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out.} Nobody commented on the sign or the date or the red edge; the two women bargaining over short weight went on standing side by side without making their figures agree.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 4: Days 5 and 6. Came under the Vail roof on Stone 11 to see the child she delivered, reached for the slate before him, pressed the fold flat at his shoulder longer than a fold required, touched the tin inside her bodice, crossed two fingers at the red edge of the flower at his wrist without knowing he saw it, and gave exact dates where the neighbour mother asked for comfort: \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out.} Called the rekindled child’s second chill a graft settling and wrote on her own slate what she then turned writing-down on the bench. On Stone 12, in the death-house, touched the tin again, wrote a second note, turned it down and slid it under a milk cup, crossed the sign at a red mark at the child’s hairline, and went on giving dates after the questions had stopped. Neither note was read and the tin was not opened.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 6: Day 10, Stone 16. Came under the Vail roof at mid-morning with soap and warm milk on her and the birth-slates under her arm; reached for the slate before the child and laid it writing-down on the bench. Pressed the fold flat at his shoulder too long, touched the little tin once inside her bodice, and crossed two fingers at the red edge of the branching mark at his wrist without knowing she did it in front of him. Covered the sign with \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out}, then with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End and a potter’s third child in Stonemouth, going on after there was no question to stop. Took up a narrow slate and wrote on it what she did not leave lying about, then turned it writing-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in her house he does not know. Said \emph{Warm and breathing --- that’s all I’ve set down} to Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet}. The tin was touched once and never opened; the note was not read.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 7: Day 18, Stone 24, came under the Vail roof at mid-morning with soap and warm milk and the smell of lye on her, the birth-slates under her arm; laid them writing-down on the bench before she turned to the fold and pressed the fold flat at his shoulder longer than a fold required. Reached once to the little tin inside her bodice and came away without opening it. Saw the red edge of the birth-flower where the wool had ridden back, crossed two fingers at the corner of it before she knew she had done it, and covered the sign with \emph{Stone seven; the account went up on the eighth, before the paper went out}, then with the cooper’s seventh in Mud End and a potter’s third child in Stonemouth, going on after there was no question left. Said \emph{Warm and breathing --- that’s all I’ve set down} to Sella’s \emph{he lies quiet}, which was exact and not true. Took up a narrow slate, wrote what she did not leave lying about in a second hand, and turned it writing-down into her shawl toward a floorboard in a house the boy could not name, where a further note would go into the tin still unread. Three doors down Dessa’s cough went on being weather.

\end{itemize}

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item Ch 8: Days 27 and 28. On the Long Night sat in the dark under the Vail roof with the fire out and told the hearth-maid’s account in which dates stand where wonder should be, going on after the question had stopped; made the two-finger sign at the red edge of his wrist without knowing it. On the Remembering came under the roof with the birth-slates and the smell of soap and warm milk, laid an exact date where a name should stand, touched the tin once inside her bodice without opening it, pressed the fold flat too long at his shoulder, crossed two fingers at the red edge of the birth-flower before she knew she had done it, and covered the sign with the same unasked-for date she had given Dessa. Wrote no new note and went home to a house the boy cannot name; offstage on the Last Day and Ilmen 1, and the lie went on standing.

On Ilmen 14 stood with Orra Weir in the lee of the Eel House, gave the date of the last high water, touched the tin once and came away empty, and let a figure for the traps change into weather; nothing was said of the third day. No new note was written and the tin stayed shut. The lie told to Dessa is now a fact in a dead woman’s face that nobody can correct.

\CRcharacter{Orra Weir}{the woman who keeps the traps and counts the names}{build/portraits/orra-weir.pdf}{\CRfield{Also called}{Orra, Orra of the Weir, the trap-keeper}\CRfield{Role}{ally}\CRfield{Born}{Y.H. 778, the Weir, Grath}\CRfield{Kind}{human (Grathic)}\CRfield{Origin}{the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, Grath}\CRfield{Allegiance}{the eel traps at the Weir; the Fish Blessing; House Weir}\CRfield{Status}{alive — the long vigil held at the Weir through Tallow 20 (Day 169), the word forty still unspoken and the forty-first double turn still legible and unnamed; gave the ninth of Ilmen, the boat of six oars and the man at the stern where a figure was asked on Day 167, her thumb’s return still undecided}\CRfield{First seen}{Chapter 10}}{\CRsheetheading{Appearance}
Thirty-four, with hands like old rope and a grey streak through black hair from a winter she spent on the weir when she was twenty and would do again. Eel scars lie across both forearms in pale arcs, and she never covers them, because a trap-keeper without scars is a trap-keeper who does not work. She smells of river silt, cold fish and tallow smoke, and in the spring of wet mud so strongly that people at the Cross know she has come before they see her. She keeps her accounts in knots on a cord of grey wool and will not sit at a table where a slate is open; she learned the habit from a Fen woman who sold her reed and taught her that a written name is a name somebody else can read. The thing people notice first is the grey streak; the thing they notice last is the cord, which she touches when a number is spoken.

\CRsheetheading{Voice \& Manner}
Slow, and when she is tired the nasal half-song of the Fen comes into it, which she has never entirely lost. She tells a story sideways and gives a date where another person would give an opinion. She never answers a question about the levy directly, but she will tell you which night the collector’s boat came and how many oars it had. When she is lying she ties a knot, which is invisible to anyone who does not know the cord.

\begin{itemize}[leftmargin=1.4em,itemsep=1pt,topsep=3pt,parsep=0pt]

\item “I don’t keep names on slate. Slates burn. Knots don’t.”

\item “Forty. I tied forty knots in the year of the flower. I tied one more and I don’t know what to call it.”

\item “The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried.”

\item “A trap works because the eel can’t see the way out. That’s all a trap is. Don’t make it more than that.”

\item “You’re the Vail boy. You’ve got her eyes and somebody else’s listening.”

\item “The ninth of Ilmen. The collector’s boat came round the bend on the flood and had six oars. One man stood at the stern and never touched them.” --- given on Reed 18 where a levy figure was asked; to \emph{That isn’t the levy}, \emph{It’s a date. The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried.}

\end{itemize}

\CRsheetheading{History}
She was born at the Weir, one league upriver of Sill, where the eel traps stand on a plank walk and the Fish Blessing is held on Ilmen 15. She has kept the traps since she was eighteen, knows the river’s moods better than the weather, and can tell a collector’s boat by its oars before it comes round the bend. She married a man who went downriver with a cart of pots and never came back, and has not looked for him, which she calls \emph{not being a fool about it}. Her son Kess was one of the forty children of Low Kiln banked in the first weeks of Stone, Y.H. 812. No return has been announced for him. She tied forty knots that year and then tied a forty-first, because on the night the children were taken she saw Sella Vail carry a covered bundle up the Clay Yard, and the bundle was small and warm and had a flower on it, and she could not account for it.

She was in the room on Stone 7 when the child with the branching red flower was born, and she saw the collector’s slate that night, and saw a name written on it before anyone had seen the infant’s face. She cannot spell the name; she remembers its shape, which is a thing no Court clerk can take away.

\CRsheetheading{Wounds \& Fears}
A son spent for a return that never came. She has gone to the Bone Orchard twice looking for a shallow grave with his name on it and found none, which is worse than finding one, because it means his warmth was banked and not wasted and is somewhere in an account she will never see. She fears the Weighing, where whole returns are announced in a clean voice to people whose children are not coming back. She fears that the forty-first knot is a thing she has made into a mystery because a plain answer would be too ordinary: the boy she saw carried was simply another child, and she has needed him not to be. Her contradiction: she sells eels to the Court’s clerk and hates the Court, and has learned the collector’s schedule in order to avoid him and also in order to be there when he comes.

\CRsheetheading{Desires}
She wants her son returned whole, which she knows will not happen, and she wants somebody else to say his name who is not herself. She thinks she wants to know what happened to the boy in the covered bundle. What she needs is to understand that a mother’s account is never settled by a return, whole or thin, and that the knot cord is not a ledger but a way of continuing to hold on to something the Court has already booked.

\CRsheetheading{Bonds}
\textbf{Kess} — her son, one of the Forty. She has a knot for him and no return, and has begun to speak to the knot in the evening, which she knows is not sensible and does not stop.

\textbf{Corin} — the Vail boy. She sees something in him that belongs to the year of the flower and cannot place it: the way he turns his head, the mark under his sleeve, the attention of a person much older than his body. She has never said this to anyone except the cord.

\textbf{Sella Vail} — she blames Sella for taking a child at the very moment forty others were taken, and has never said why she blames her, which leaves the blame floating free and available for anything.

\textbf{Dessa Silt} — they were both in the room on Stone 7. Dessa believes her baby died; Orra knows she is lying and has not said. It is the one thing she has never sold at the Fishstairs.

\textbf{Alda Reed} — the only person with whom she has ever discussed the third day. They do not discuss the birth-flower. They discuss the weather and the river and occasionally the number forty, and then one of them touches something and the subject changes.

\textbf{Mira Silt} — her eel buyer, her friend, and the one person she lets near the knots. Mira wants the secret out; Orra wants it kept, which is the only disagreement in a friendship of fifteen years.

\textbf{Berr Clay, the Thane of Clay} — bought her eels for the levy feast and paid two marks short. She has never forgiven the arithmetic, and has served him the same short measure ever since.

\textbf{Ch 10.} Her first appearance is moved forward from the planned Chapter 12 to Chapter 10 so that the word \emph{forty} can land in the boy’s hearing at the Fish Blessing. She comes onstage on Ilmen 14, rope-handed and eel-scarred, smelling of silt, cold fish and tallow, telling a story sideways and giving a date where another woman would give an opinion, with the collector’s boat and its oars where a direct answer should be; her knot-accounts are in the Eel House and she will not sit at a table where a slate lies open. On Ilmen 15 she keeps the accounts in knots on grey wool, tells the boy that an eel goes into a trap and cannot find the way out, ties a forty-first knot she cannot account for over the story of a small warm covered bundle with a flower carried up the Clay Yard in the year of the flower, says \emph{forty} low into the basket and watches what he does with it. He is too young to answer. She does not know that he is the child in the bundle, and she keeps the watching. Alda stands with her in the lee of the Eel House and the third day is not spoken of; Mira keeps her own grey wool beside the knot-string without either woman saying what she knows.

\textbf{Ch 11.} She came down from the Weir on Day 45 with eels, with silt and cold fish and tallow smoke going ahead of her, pale eel scars uncovered and the grey knot-string at her waist worrying under her thumb. The boy could now read the shape of the forty-first knot --- double turn, tail tucked, tied left over right, the small extra weight of a thumb --- but not its name, and she watched him watching without saying the word a second time or asking what he had made of it. Once she tied a knot, pulled it down with her thumb and set it among the others; at the end of the morning the cord went back upriver to the Eel House, where no clerk could spell it and no boy could read it. She gave a date where another woman would have given an opinion and kept the watching, which has had no answer.

\textbf{Ch 15.} She is offstage through the flood except for one morning. On Silt 13, as the water fell, she came down from the Weir before light with silt on her boots and the smell of cold fish and tallow going ahead of her, the grey streak showing first through the black hair, the pale eel scars uncovered across both forearms and her hands like old rope. She stood at the edge where the water had gone down to the last wrinkle with her board and her cord and nothing else, set the board on its side and turned it with her wrist, the turn of a person who has done it ten thousand times, and did not speak. Once she pulled a knot down with her thumb and set it among the others and did not look into the basket. She gave a date where another woman would have given an opinion, and here there was not even a date, only the standing and the cord and the board turned on its side. The boy watched her watching him and the watching got no answer; the cord went back upriver to the Eel House where no clerk could spell it and no boy could read it, and the word was not spoken. Her board lay beside Mira’s on the Fishstairs boards and did not touch it.

\textbf{Ch 27 (bonds).} On Reed 3 she stood at the lower boards of the Weir with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, pulling one knot down with her thumb and setting it among the others. When a weir woman asked her a question about the levy she gave a date instead of an answer and went back to the knots; when the reed-cutter lifted his bundle she watched what there was to watch at the edge of the shade and got no answer from the basket. She did not ask and nobody asked her. The shape of the last knot on her cord was legible to the boy without its name and he did not spend it; the word forty stayed unspoken. Her cord lay beside Mira’s board and did not touch it, and a third private record — the reed-cutter’s tally in wool gone grey with handling — passed along the same boards unread, not joined to hers and not carried to any door. The long vigil holds: she has set a thing down in front of him and is waiting to see whether it will be picked up, and a baby with no hand that can reach a league upriver cannot pick it up. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 28 (bonds).} On Reed 6 she stood at the lower boards of the Weir with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, pulling one knot down with her thumb and setting it among the others; her hands were like old rope and the pale eel scars lay uncovered across both forearms, and the nasal half-song of the Fen came into her voice where she was tired, as it had at the blessing and every morning since. When the weir woman with salt white at her wrists asked what the levy would take now the hands were out of the reeds, Orra gave a date instead of a figure: \emph{The ninth of Ilmen. The collector’s boat came round the bend on the flood and had six oars. One man stood at the stern and never touched them.} To \emph{That isn’t the levy} she said \emph{It’s a date. The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried}, and pulled another knot down. Her thumb went to the cord again as the sentence ended, and the boy could not tell whether that was a lie or only the habit of counting and did not make a cause of it. When the reed-cutter lifted his bundle off the stone she watched what there was to watch at the edge of the shade and got no answer from the basket; nobody asked her and she did not ask. The shape of the last knot on her cord was legible without its name — double turn, tail tucked, left over right, the small extra weight of a thumb — and the boy did not spend it. Her board lay beside Mira’s eel board and did not touch it; the reed-cutter’s tally went past unread, a third private record not joined to hers. The word forty stayed unspoken and the long vigil held: she has set a thing down in front of him and is waiting to see whether it will be picked up, and a baby with no hand that can reach a league upriver cannot pick it up. No new scar, possession or change of voice.

\textbf{Ch 29 (bonds).} On Reed 9 she stood at the lower boards of the Weir with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, turning the board with the wrist that had turned it ten thousand times. Her hands were like old rope and the pale eel scars lay uncovered across both forearms; the grey streak showed first through the black hair when she moved her head, and the nasal half-song she had never lost came into her voice where she was tired. She pulled one knot down with her thumb and set it among the others. When a woman at the rails asked what the levy would take now the hands were out of the reeds, she gave a date instead of a figure: \emph{The ninth of Ilmen. The collector’s boat came round the bend on the flood and had six oars. One man stood at the stern and never touched them.} To \emph{That isn’t the levy} she said \emph{It’s a date. The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried}, and went back to the knots. Her thumb went to the cord again as the sentence ended, and the boy could not tell whether that was a lie or only the habit of counting and did not make a cause of it. A date given where a figure was asked was an answer with the question taken out of it, a chart closed over a note nobody had opened, and he set it where it belonged; the man at the stern who kept his hands off the oars was set on a place of its own, apart from the midwife’s reaching hand and the thane’s twice-wiped thumb, and no cause written across the three. The reed-cutter tied one knot low with his teeth on the blessing stone and said \emph{You can ask the cord} / \emph{No more can the Court}; she watched what there was to watch and got no answer from the basket, and did not ask and was not asked. \textbf{Ch 31 (bonds).} On Days 132 and 134 she stood at the lower boards of the Weir with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, turning it with the wrist that has turned it ten thousand times; her hands were like old rope, the pale eel scars lay uncovered across both forearms and the nasal half-song of the Fen came into her voice where she was tired. She pulled one knot down with her thumb and set it among the others. Asked what the levy would take now the hands were out in the reeds she gave a date where another woman would give a figure: \emph{The ninth of Ilmen. The collector’s boat came round the bend on the flood and had six oars. One man stood at the stern and never touched them}; to \emph{That isn’t the levy} she said \emph{It’s a date. The river takes what the Court doesn’t. You can shout at either one. I’ve tried}, and went back to the knots. Her thumb went to the cord again at the end of the sentence and the boy could not tell whether it was a lie or the habit of counting and made no cause of it. The man who stands at the stern keeping his hands off the oars is set on a place of its own apart from the midwife’s reaching hand, the thane’s twice-wiped thumb and the record-first hand that enters a figure before it looks for the man who said it. The reed-cutter tied one knot low with his teeth on the flat blessing stone, bit the end off and put his grey cord back inside his coat; she watched what there was to watch and got no answer from the basket, and did not ask and was not asked. Her knot-string lay beside Mira Silt’s eel board and did not touch it; the last knot showed its double turn, tail tucked, tied left over right with the small extra weight of a thumb pressed in, and the word that would have named it stayed unspoken. The long vigil held.

\textbf{Ch 32 (bonds).} On Day 137 she stood at the lower boards of the Weir with her board on its side and a cord at her waist, turning it with the wrist that has turned it ten hundred times, hands like old rope and the pale eel scars uncovered across both forearms, the grey streak showing first through the black hair. She pulled one knot down with her thumb and set it among the others. To the woman who asked what the levy would take now the hands were out in the reeds she gave a date --- \emph{The ninth of Ilmen. The collector’s boat came round the bend on the flood and had six oars. One man stood at the stern and never touched them} --- and, told that was not the levy, \emph{It’s a date. Mira’s board lay beside hers and did not touch it, and neither woman’s knots were counted.
